headline: Cemetery Commission approved new green burial lot pricing and reviewed Section 8 development plans and bulk lot purchasing issues.
summary: The commission welcomed new commissioner Miles McCallum, discussed a proposed family interment policy for multi-generational lots, and approved new pricing for green burial lots. Staff gave updates on the Section 8 cemetery expansion plan and discussed whether to allow bulk lot purchases, including a possible sale to the Islamic Society of Vermont (ISVT).
decisions: Approved the proposed green burial lot pricing structure, setting resident rate at $1765 and non-resident rate at $2808 per lot.

decision_evidence.quote: Diaz feels comfortable with the current proposed pricing. She asked if all were in favor of the proposed pricing structure. The motion passed unanimously.

plain_text:
Cemetery Superintendent/BPRW Director: Cindi Wight 
  Chair: Jennifer Diaz 
 Vice-chair – Alexandra Millar  
  
 
 
City of Burlington    455 North Avenue    Burlington, Vermont 05401    (802) 863-2075 
 
Cemetery Commission Meeting Minutes 
 
 
Meeting Date:  September 17, 2026 
 
Commissioners Present: Jennifer Diaz, Nancy, Kirby, Miles McCallum, Alexandra Millar-House, Mary 
Wesley 
 
Staff Present: Holli Bushnell, Steve Bachand, Sophie Sauve 
 
Meeting was called to order 4:38pm at by Chair Jennifer Diaz 
 
I. Approval of Agenda 
Diaz moved to adopt the agenda, Mary Wesley and Alexandra Millar-House moved to second, all 
were in favor 
 
II. Approval of minutes from 6/18/2026 
Diaz moved to approve the minutes, Miles McCallum seconded, all were in favor 
 
III. Public Forum 
Public forum was opened at 4:54pm, as no one was present or wished to speak, public forum 
was also closed at 4:54pm 
 
IV. Welcoming New Commissioner 
Miles McCallum introduced himself.  He shared that he is coming to the commission from a 
historic preservation based perspective and is very interested in working at Elmwood.  The rest 
of the commission introduced themselves to McCallum, sharing a bit about their interests.  
Steve Bachand and Sophie Sauve introduced themselves as well.  McCallum concluded his 
introduction by inviting the commission to a grave themed event at the Burlington History and 
Cultural Center.   
 
V. Family Interment Policy 
Bachand emailed everyone a copy of proposed interment policy. He explained that there have 
been issues with multi-generational lots that have led to disputes about who can and cannot be 
buried in the graves.  The questions we have come up with are, should the decision require a 
majority of owners to agree or should it be 100% agreement from the all family members within 
the current generation of ownership.  Bachand then related a story of a family where the 
parents purchased a multi-grave lot and then both had passed.  After their passing, their four 
children would be considered owners of the lot by our current policy.  One of the siblings passed
Page 2 of 6 
away and her son wished to inter her with her parents.  Two brothers agreed to have the 
deceased sister buried in the lot, but the remaining sister did not agree.  This turned into a legal 
battle and is one of the main reasons we are looking to set a policy.   
Diaz shared that she feels the most prudent and fair way is if the Power of Attorney for the 
deceased to be interred should have the decision deferred to them.  This is a final resting place.  
There should not be a fight. 
Bachand added that, in his personal opinion, we are not and cannot be a family court.  If the 
family can’t figure it out then there is no burial.  It’s such a tough call and it’s hard to find the 
right answer.   
McCallum asked what the parameters are for who counts as family.  He likes the idea of having 
the POA be the final arbiter because it sidesteps the parameters of “family.” 
Bushnell explained that, in our current policy, one someone purchases a lot they and their 
spouse are considered owners (unless otherwise specified).  When the original owners pass, the 
lot then passes to the next generation, the children of the original owners (she encourages new 
purchasers to designate a point person or new owner in their wills).  Once everyone from the 
children’s generation passes, lots will then be owned by any and all grandchildren.  This is why 
we have some lots that require the agreement of over a dozen people for burial to take place.   
Diaz felt that it makes sense to have a legal person be the determinant factor if a dispute arises 
(a POA or other legal representative).  
Bachand explained that we now use a lot purchase agreement which contains language to 
prevent this from happening in the future.  We now ask for owners to designate “people 
approved to be buried in the lot” and “People (other than Lot owners) authorized to schedule 
grave openings” in hopes of mitigating this issue in the future. 
Diaz asked if the form should also as for POA information.   
Bachand felt that that would be a question for the city attorney.  Unfortunately Hayley was not 
able to join the meeting today.  Bachand asked commissioners to email Steve and/or Hayley 
with their questions.   
 
VI. Green Burial Fees (action) 
Bachand shared the proposal for new pricing.  We are getting close to making green burial lots 
available for purchase.  At the moment, our regular size graves are 3 1/2’ by 11’ or 38.5 sqft.  
This works out to $29.43 per square foot, and that is what we’re basing the green burial lot price 
on.  Green lots are 5’x 12’, and for a space that is 60 sqft the cost should be $1765 based on the 
existing square footage rate.  This is also true for the non-residents rate (currently $46.81 per 
sqft).  For non-residents, green burial lots should be $2808.  That’s what staff is proposing to 
charge for green burials 
Diaz asked how our rates compare to other cemeteries.
Page 3 of 6 
Bachand explained that North Hero charges $400 for their lots, and they really just made that 
price up.  The proposed rate is based on the square footage pricing we’re charging now.  To him 
that seems like the fairest way to figure it out.   
McCallum asked if there is a reason green burial lots are larger.   
Bachand explained that 5 ½’ x 12’ is the standard size nationwide for green/natural burial so 
that will be the policy we will follow.   
Diaz asked if the prices listed were the total cost for interment or just the lot purchase price. 
Bushnell interjected that it is just the lot purchase price. 
Bachand continued that we’re going to have a sort of menu for people.  There will be lots of 
options for lowering.  We’ve learned from other green cemeteries that traditional lowering 
devices do not work for green burial.  We will have options for families like hemp rope, pine 
boards, wood chips, and other things that that will be added on to the final burial price.  
Bachand will send the policy to everyone to review and is happy to answer questions. 
Diaz shared that she quickly searched for city cemetery pricing for burials and found that our 
rates are pretty comparable to the national average.   
Millar-House asked if the pricing will limit who is able to purchase these lots.  The rates are cost 
prohibitive for a lot of people 
Wesley appreciates the way the new prices were calculated.  She also reminded the commission 
that there are some things about green burial that will be less expensive (no embalming, no 
casket, etc…) 
Diaz feels comfortable with the current proposed pricing. She asked if all were in favor of the 
proposed pricing structure.  The motion passed unanimously.  Bachand will bring the proposal to 
Board of Finance and the City Council for approval through them and then we should be all set 
to move forward.   
 
VII. Section 8 Plan (update) 
Sophie Sauve was present to share an update on the Section 8 work.  The project has been going 
on for a couple of years and we are now in a place where we need to push the project forward 
because we are starting to run out of grass roads to convert into burial space.  Section 8 is the 
last(ish) undeveloped area in the cemetery. It’s a great area with beautiful lake view and old 
growth trees.   
 
Part of the development of Section 8 was an attempt at maximizing space and providing options 
for updated burial trends.  Some of the mature trees will die out, as they are near the end of 
their lifespan anyway, but the plan does attempt to maintain the existing canopy.  In terms of 
traditional burials vs cremation burials vs green, we would be adding 138 traditional lots, 208 
green burial lots, 772 cremation burial lots (with room for two cremains in each lot).  1544 
spaces total, 772 total lots.  There will be no burials on the ravine side of the section.  In center
Page 4 of 6 
there is a plan for cremation lots with tall column monument like what exists in the Louisa 
Howard Cremation Garden.  The plans call for green burial lots across from the existing Muslim 
section. There is space for future columbariums should we choose to purchase them.  The plans 
feature a central ossuary with chamber for ashes to go into rather than scatter garden with 
seating all around central area and great lake view.  The plans also call for formalizing the roads 
around the section so maintenance crews can do their jobs.   
Millar-House asked if Sauve could you speak to changes from last time the commission saw the 
plan.  Sauve shared that a big changes is the triangle area in the northeast part of the section.  
Initially, one family wanted to purchase that space to move a private mausoleum onto, but 
we’ve changed that are into cremation options that will accommodate multiple people/families.  
The walkways have been widened for better accessibility.  It was also discussed that we may add 
a pillar obelisk to accommodating green burial folks who want a marker.  There is a question of 
if we actually want more columbariums or if those reserved areas would be more effective as in-
ground burial space.   
In terms of development we intend to start with the northern area.  The next steps are pinning 
most of section so we can start selling the lots.  There are also some burial locations that were 
identified as being too close to mature trees, so those were removed.  Once those mature trees 
die off we can use their footprint for burial space.  Some of section used for leaf debris so we 
will still have a dirt/junk pile for maintenance.   
Millar-House noted that the green burial graves in the north section are still oriented towards 
Mecca.  She wondered if the Islamic Society’s decided that they would like green burial lots.  
Bachand explained that those green burial lots are going to remain for green burials.  ISVT has 
long been advocating for more graves, and we’ll be able to accommodate them in this new plan.  
Bachand will be meeting on 9/30 with ISVT and will know much more after that.  The plan is to 
keep the proposed lots as green burial lots whether it becomes a Muslim section or not.  The 
city attorneys have determined that Muslims can’t have their own section anymore unless they 
purchase them outright.  They are not going to like it, but it’s what we would do for any large 
religious group.   
Diaz commented that purchasing the lots has point of contention for quite some time.  She’s 
looking forward to hearing how the meeting goes.  Bachand feels cautiously optimistic that we’ll 
move forward.   
 
VIII. Bulk Lot Purchasing (discussion) 
This particular topic comes back to the ongoing conversation about new section and green 
burial lots.  We are no longer allowed to have a religious specific section (unless those religious 
groups purchase their lots outright).  In order for ISVT to have their own section, they need to 
bulk purchase.  Should we allow them to do that?  We’ve never denied bulk purchases before.
Page 5 of 6 
Howard Dean bought dozens of lots back in 2014.  It would be wrong to say no and not offer 
that to them.   
Millar recalled that the issue we’re running into is that we do not want to allow bulk purchase of 
green burial lots.  So if we’re offering a bulk purchase of a green burial section does that mean 
we have to allow bulk purchases in another section. 
Bachand countered that we also have to take into consideration that ISVT has asked us for more 
graves.  
Diaz felt that if ISVT decides they want all the lots and to have them be green lots, then it turns 
into a Muslim section. 
Millar asked if the language on the map indicates lots that are not green burial for green burial 
would that prevent the issue.  She explained that she was trying to find ways that we can meet 
ISVT’s need for a bulk purchase in a way that feels fair/equitable.  She specifically referenced the 
triangle area across from the existing Muslim section 
Bachand explained that if someone came in tomorrow and wanted to buy the triangle for green 
burials we would allow it.  But that’s because there’s no existing graves in the triangle.  We can’t 
do traditional and green burials next to each other.  So a bulk purchase of an undeveloped area 
is the only way they could get around that.  In a non-green part of section 8 we would not allow 
a bulk purchase of lots for green burial.  They would need to purchase in the green section. 
Millar-House felt that that distinction might need to be clarified in internal documents.   
Bushnell pondered if it would be possible to sell square footage to ISVT instead of lots.   
Diaz wondered if there are Muslims who want traditional burial.    Bachand explained that, if 
we’re going to sell 67 or 148 graves to ISVT, then we have to allow someone to buy all the green 
lots if they want.  If we allow ISVT to do this do we have to allow individuals to bulk purchase.  
We’ve done it before.  The issue is that we have a very limited number of green burial lots.  The 
total number is 208.  By allowing ISVT to buy 67 would that mean we then allow someone to 
purchase the other 141 green lots?   
Millar-House reiterated that, because this is basically the last developable area of any of our 
cemeteries we’ve talked about no bulk purchases at all.  Bulk purchases take away from 
mandate to serve the city population.  
Bachand explained that no one knows how quickly we’ll sell these lots.  With green burials we 
will be picking the grave, so we’re selling burial rights (not how it works for traditional lots).  
Also keep in mind that we can change things in the future.  We could convert traditional graves 
into green graves in other parts of Section 8. 
Millar-House asked if we do not intend to open the whole section at once.  Bachand confirmed 
that this was the case. We may strategically say in house “hold these rows.” 
McCallum felt that, in regard to bulk purchasing, we don’t have an official policy, we’re just 
working on precedent.  If ISVT wants to bulk buy, they can because we’ve set that precedent 
before.  To kick the can down the road a bit we could offer the bulk purchase option to ISVT,
Page 6 of 6 
allow them to do what they want, and then make the policy official.   Bachand explained that 
this discussion with ISVT could drag on for another 6 months.  But, to recap, we could make this 
sale to ISVT and then develop a bulk buying policy where the policy officially decided after ISVT 
purchase is completed.   
Diaz asked if there would be issues with symantics of labeling the section “Muslim.”  Bachand 
didn’t think it would matter because the graves would already sold at that point.   
Diaz felt that this conversation will be on going.   
 
IX. Adjournment 
The meeting was adjourned at 5:58pm.  Diaz moved, Wesley seconded, and all were in favor.  
The next meeting will be held on October 22, 2026 at the Lakeview Cemetery office and via 
zoom at 4:30pm
